\begin{tablenotes}[flushleft]
\footnotesize
\item[] \textit{Note:} The linear cost, equation \eqref{eq:esc:budget}; $\rho = 1$ is log preferences. Panel A: the derivative of the political objective of the electorate of 1990 in the design it chooses for 2020, eq.\ \eqref{eq:esc:leadFOC}, at the U.S.\ choice $\theta_{2020} = 0.544$, by route: the design with the share of revenue lost and the anticipated tax held, which pulls the design towards flat benefits; the dependence of the share lost on the design (eq.\ \eqref{eq:esc:ftheta}), the saving on the loss; and the response of the anticipated tax $\mathcal{T}_{2020}(\theta_{2020})$. The routes sum to zero at the choice; each share is one of the last two routes over their sum, which offsets the pull. Panel B: $\theta_{2020}$ on the path where the choice binds from the first period, as France\textquotesingle s income distribution is imposed on the U.S., first everywhere but in the cost, whose share of revenue lost at each design is held at its U.S.\ value, then in the dispersion of relative incomes $\tilde{V}$ in the cost, and last in the tax rate in the cost; the first step is the combined effect of France\textquotesingle s distribution outside the cost, and the total is the response to France\textquotesingle s income distribution in figure \ref{fig:US_ESC:overview}. In the first two steps $\lambda$ is multiplied at each date by a factor, taken as given by voters, that equates the share lost at the tax rate of the path solved with the share at the U.S.\ tax rate of that date, so that at a candidate tax off the path the share lost still changes in proportion to the tax rate. Under CRRA preferences the share held is met to a relative gap of at most 0.12\%. The dispersion in the cost alone is the U.S.\ with France\textquotesingle s $\tilde{V}$ in the cost, computed under log preferences only. Panel C: the magnitudes of appendix \ref{app:esc:cost}, $\pi = \Pi/R$ on the path without the cost, $\lambda$ of table \ref{table:US_ESC:calibration}, and $\varepsilon = \lambda/\pi$ the elasticity of the base that $\lambda = \varepsilon\pi$ implies under a constant elasticity. $\lambda$ at $\varepsilon$ is the cost parameter $\varepsilon\pi$ that an elasticity $\varepsilon$ implies, at the ends of the range of participation and taxable-income elasticities \parencite{ChettyGMW11a1,SaezSG12a1}, and the multiples are the calibrated $\lambda$ over it.
\end{tablenotes}
